lesson.title: Sliding Downhill: The Mirror Image of Increasing
lesson.summary: A function is decreasing on an interval when its output values fall as the input moves to the right, which the First Derivative Test detects as f prime being negative there.
lesson.body:
A function f is decreasing on an interval I if, for every pair a and b in I with a less than b, f(a) is greater than f(b). Tracing the graph left to right, the curve only goes downhill. This is the direct mirror image of the increasing function definition from the previous section, and the same Mean Value Theorem argument applies with the inequality flipped: if f'(x) is less than 0 for every x in an interval, then f is decreasing there.

Return to f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 and its derivative f'(x) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1), with critical numbers at x = -1 and x = 3. The sign chart already built for that function showed f'(0) = -9, a negative value, for the middle interval (-1, 3). Testing any other point in that interval gives the same negative sign, for instance f'(1) = 3(1 - 3)(1 + 1) = 3(-2)(2) = -12, also negative. So f is decreasing on (-1, 3), or equivalently on the closed interval [-1, 3] if the critical numbers are included by convention.

Graphically, this means the cubic climbs up to a peak at x = -1, where f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1)^2 - 9(-1) + 5 = -1 - 3 + 9 + 5 = 10, then slides downhill all the way to a valley at x = 3, where f(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 5 = -22, before climbing again. The switch from increasing to decreasing at x = -1 and from decreasing back to increasing at x = 3 is not a coincidence: it is exactly how the First Derivative Test locates local maxima and minima, and it sets up the idea of monotonicity covered next, where increasing and decreasing behavior are stitched together into one complete picture of a function's shape.
